overview.title: Smaller model vs. original: figure 5.18
overview.main_topic: Completing the lower-capacity IMDb model (4-4-1), comparing its validation loss with the 16-16-1 reference, and starting the high-capacity (512-unit) variant
overview.central_idea: Cutting the hidden layers from 16 to 4 units delays overfitting (it begins after about six epochs instead of four) and makes validation loss degrade more slowly afterwards. The page then sets up the opposite experiment with a model far larger than the problem warrants.
overview.importance: Figure 5.18 is the first empirical evidence in the book that reducing capacity is a regularizer. It turns the 'compressed representations' argument of p.185 into a measured curve.

summary:
The page completes **Listing 5.11**, the lower-capacity model, which began on p.186. Both hidden layers are `Dense(4, activation="relu")`, followed by `Dense(1, activation="sigmoid")`. Compilation (`rmsprop`, `binary_crossentropy`, accuracy) and training (20 epochs, batch size 512, `validation_split=0.4`) are exactly as in the reference listing 5.10. The result is stored as `history_smaller_model`.

**Figure 5.18** plots the validation loss of both models over 20 epochs. The original model (red dashed line) drops quickly to a minimum of about 0.28 around epoch 4, then climbs steadily to about 0.56 by epoch 20. The smaller model (solid line) starts higher (about 0.49 at epoch 1) because it learns more slowly, reaches its minimum of roughly 0.27-0.28 a few epochs later, and then rises only gently, to about 0.38 at epoch 20. The authors summarize: **the smaller model starts overfitting later than the reference model (after six epochs rather than four), and its performance degrades more slowly once it starts overfitting.**

The authors then turn to the other extreme: "let's add to our benchmark a model that has much more capacity, far more than the problem warrants." **Listing 5.12, "Version of the model with higher capacity"**, begins at the bottom of the page with `layers.Dense(512, activation="relu")`. The rest (a second 512-unit layer and the same compile/fit, stored as `history_larger_model`) is on p.188, together with figure 5.19.

concepts.name: Model capacity
concepts.definition: The number of learnable parameters, and so the model's ability to memorize. Here it is varied through the hidden-layer width.
concepts.intuition: Fewer units means less room to memorize individual reviews, so the model has to rely on general word-sentiment patterns.
concepts.technical: The 4-4-1 model has 40,029 parameters, against 160,305 for 16-16-1. Most of them are in the first layer (10,000 x 4 + 4).
concepts.significance: Figure 5.18 shows that capacity controls when and how strongly overfitting happens.
concepts.example: 4 units per layer: overfitting starts after about 6 epochs. 16 units: after about 4.
concepts.misconception: A smaller model is not automatically better. If it is too small it underfits and its best validation loss is worse (p.185).

concepts.name: Overfitting (as seen in a validation curve)
concepts.definition: The regime where training continues to improve training loss but validation loss gets worse.
concepts.intuition: The model starts learning facts about specific training reviews instead of general sentiment cues.
concepts.technical: Visible as the U-shape of the val_loss curve. The minimum marks the best-generalizing epoch, and the slope after it measures how fast overfitting proceeds.
concepts.significance: Both the onset epoch and the post-minimum slope are used on this page to compare models.
concepts.example: Original model val_loss: about 0.28 at epoch 4, about 0.56 at epoch 20.
concepts.misconception: Overfitting is not a single moment. It is a process whose speed depends on capacity.

concepts.name: Size reduction as regularization
concepts.definition: Using fewer parameters to make the model less able to fit the training set perfectly, so it generalizes better.
concepts.intuition: A narrower pipe can only carry the main stream, not every drop.
concepts.technical: This restricts the hypothesis class. The effect on the curves is a delayed, flatter overfitting phase.
concepts.significance: It is the first of the three techniques in 5.4.4, followed by weight regularization (p.189) and dropout (p.190).
concepts.misconception: You do not need fewer layers to regularize. Here the depth stays the same and only the width shrinks.

deeper.title: Reading figure 5.18 carefully
deeper.body:
These are approximate readings from the plot (not values stated in the text):

- **Original model**: about 0.40 at epoch 1, minimum about 0.28 near epoch 4, then a noisy climb to about 0.56 at epoch 20.
- **Smaller model**: about 0.49 at epoch 1 (it learns more slowly), minimum about 0.275 around epochs 6-8, then a gentle rise to about 0.38 at epoch 20.

Three lessons follow. (1) The minimum shifts later. (2) The post-minimum slope is much flatter. (3) The best validation losses of the two models are similar here, so the smaller model is not clearly *better* at its best epoch, only more *forgiving* if you train too long. The book's text states the first two points. The third is an inference from the plot.

deeper.title: Why less capacity means slower overfitting
deeper.body: Beyond the book: every gradient step has to share 4 hidden features across all 15,000 training reviews. To lower the loss on many reviews at once, those features have to capture broadly useful signals (for example, 'contains strongly positive words'). Fitting one odd review would require dedicating a feature to it, at the expense of the others. With 16, or 512, features there is spare capacity to do exactly that, so memorization starts earlier.

deeper.title: Analogy: a small notebook
deeper.body: A student allowed a one-page cheat sheet must write down general principles. A student allowed a hundred pages can copy every worked example verbatim, then fails on new questions. The 4-unit model has the one-page cheat sheet.

questions.question: What does figure 5.18 show about the smaller (4-unit) model compared with the original?
options: It overfits earlier and more severely
It starts overfitting later (about six epochs rather than four) and degrades more slowly
It has lower validation loss at every epoch
questions.answer: It starts overfitting later (about six epochs rather than four) and degrades more slowly
questions.explanation: This is the book's own reading of the figure. It does overfit eventually (so 'never overfits' is wrong), and in the first epochs its loss is higher (so 'every epoch' is wrong). Earlier and more severe overfitting describes the larger model on p.188.

questions.question: Why is the smaller model's validation loss higher than the original's during the first two or three epochs?
questions.answer: With fewer units it fits the data more slowly. Its limited capacity means each epoch reduces the loss less, so early on it is still underfitting relative to the bigger model.
questions.explanation: Capacity speeds up fitting (p.188: 'the more capacity the model has, the more quickly it can model the training data'). The flip side is a slower start for small models.

questions.question: What is the only difference between listings 5.10 and 5.11?
questions.answer: The hidden layers have 4 units each instead of 16. Data, optimizer, loss, metrics, epochs, batch size and validation split are the same.
questions.explanation: Keeping everything else fixed isolates the effect of capacity.

questions.question: How many parameters does the 4-4-1 model have with 10,000 input features, and by what factor is that smaller than the 16-16-1 model's 160,305?
questions.explanation: 160,305 / 40,029 is about 4.0, because the first layer dominates and its size scales linearly with width.

questions.question: If you used early stopping (p.185) on both models, would the smaller model necessarily win? Reason from figure 5.18.
questions.answer: Not necessarily. Both curves reach similar minima (about 0.275-0.28). Early stopping would capture each model's best epoch, so the smaller model's main advantage, its slower degradation after the minimum, matters less.
questions.explanation: This is an inference from the plotted curves. The book's text emphasizes when overfitting starts and how fast it proceeds, not a lower minimum.
